At a glance: research, software, courses and tools 
 The public work of Cyril Voyant in medical physics and energy forecasting, courses and software included, each item linked to its source: paper, DOI, repository, team. Free to reuse, crediting the authors. 
 Main ideas 
 Understand before you compute Start from the human question, model the system, then choose the tool. Beat a simple reference Every forecast is first compared with persistence; a model that does not beat it adds nothing. Complexity must pay A frugal model (ELM, autoregression) first; heavier only if the gain is shown. Trust is demonstrated Public code, data, licences and verification; AI is a tool, declared. Research lines 
 Solar and energy forecasting Persistence, BLEND, ELM, dimensionality reduction, the Corsican electricity mix. 
 Evaluating forecasts NICE, γ-index, sCV and forecastability, prediction intervals. 
 Medical physics Biologically equivalent doses (LQL-Equiv), radioiodine therapy of the thyroid. 
 AI and language Language models as interfaces to validated codes. 
 Assessing research Influence index, the RTVACOS framework, scientific publishing.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/approach/

Understand before you compute: the approach of Cyril Voyant 
 Medicine, energy, language: very different questions, one method. People and their question at the center; a model we understand at the core; every tool, artificial intelligence included, around it. Complexity is added only when it brings a measurable gain. 
 Cyril Voyant · Research Director, Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E. 
 In brief 
 Compute directly when the link between inputs and outputs is known. When an explicit model falls short, hybridize : keep the model and learn only what is missing. When the useful relations are not known well enough, evaluate what the data can teach, one step of complexity at a time, and only as far as it pays. 
 Simpler is often no worse, and sometimes better: a learning machine that reads only its own satellite cell forecasts better than the same model reading the whole map, with a thousand times fewer parameters, and better than the deep networks tested. 
 AI belongs in every toolbox, not in every solution: a language model may prepare a calculation, never guess it. 
 Map of the work: four columns for the steps of the approach (direct model; hybrid, model plus learning; frugal learning; heavy learning and language models) and three rows for the fields (medicine, energy, language), each published or open work written in its cell 
 One method, every field 
 Cyril Voyant works on the dose of a radiotherapy treatment, the response of thyroid cancer to radioactive iodine, the output of a solar plant, the electricity mix of an island, the load of a road tunnel, and requests written in plain language. Medicine, energy and language are treated the same way. The domain changes; the method does not. 
 1. Start with the direct approach 
 When the link is known, compute it. Radiobiological dose equivalence follows an explicit model, checked on 4,438 treatment schedules (LQL-Equiv). When no measurements exist, the electricity demand of a tunnel is simulated from what is known about it (Tunnel Load Simulator). Before forecasting the sun, describe how variable and how forecastable a site is (sCV and F). 
 2. When the model falls short, hybridize 
 This is the route Cyril Voyant prefers. When an explicit model meets the need well enough, no learning is added without reason. When it falls short, it is completed, not replaced: learning informed by physics, medicine or mathematics estimates only what the model does not capture. 
 Thyroid cancer : a compartmental model by Marie Fusella Giuntini and Dominique Barbolosi , with Cyril Voyant and David Taieb, is the base of a hybrid digital twin now in progress ( Scientific Reports , 2026). 
 Solar forecasting : hybrid forecasts combined a numerical weather model with ARMA and neural networks as early as 2012 ( Energy , 2012); cyclostationary references write the symmetry of the signal into the forecast ( Applied Mathematical Modelling , 2026). 
 3. When relations are not known well enough, learn, only as far as it pays 
 Persistence, then structured references (BLEND, CLIPER, ARTU), statistical models, frugal learning machines (ELM), and only then deep networks or foundation models. Each step is kept only if it beats the previous one under the same protocol. 
 One ELM forecasts seven signals of the Corsican grid at once, one hour ahead, with nRMSE 0.179 for solar and 0.051 for thermal ( Applied Energy , 2026). 
 Removing the clear-sky model makes the forecasting chain simpler, and the ELM matches or outperforms the classical references ( Solar Energy , 2025). 
 4. Artificial intelligence, in its place 
 Machine learning, deep learning and language models are valuable and used every day. They remain tools around an understood, validated core. In WebSemantic, a language model reads the request, a validator asks whenever an input is missing, and a validated code computes every number. Using AI in a lab also means rules: what the European AI Act asks of research, who is responsible when a model leaves the lab, and a toolbox for researchers ( AI in research ). 
 5. Trust is demonstrated 
 Every result is judged against a reference with metrics that match the question (NICE, the γ-index), and published with its code, data and limits, archived with a DOI. Research must be found, trusted and reused: this is the point of the RTVACOS framework on research excellence. The same questioning applies to research itself: with J. P. A. Ioannidis (Stanford University), J. Baas and R. Boverhof (Elsevier), institutions are mapped by impact next to research-integrity proxies ( Royal Society Open Science , 2026), and influence is read against an explicit 2 % baseline rather than by volume ( questioning how we do research ). 
 The five principles 
 People at the center : forecasts and calculations serve a human decision. 
 The model at the core : understand first; compute directly; hybridize when the model falls short. 
 Complexity only if it pays : no a priori on the method; start simple. 
 Every tool, at the periphery : AI included, often in hybrid form. 
 Trust is demonstrated : evaluation, open code, data and limits. 
 Go further 
 The reference page, with every source (for researchers and machines): https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/approach.html 
 Methods and code , with full theory and runnable examples: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/ 
 Author profile : person.cyrilvoyant.com · ORCID 0000-0003-0242-7377

Scientific publishing: no verification, no trust 
 How can verification become as visible as publication? The number of indexed articles grew by about 47% between 2016 and 2022 [1] , peer review relies on unpaid work, and generative AI makes plausible text almost free. The answer is not more journals: it is to check the data and code behind what is published, with the same rigour Europe now demands of AI systems. 
 Four numbers, four sources 
 Indexed articles (Scopus, Web of Science), 2016 = 100 
 Hanson et al. 2024 [1] 
 Share of papers published by the top five publishers 
 Larivière et al. 2015 [2] 
 Papers retracted in 2023, and those of one publisher 
 Van Noorden 2023 [5] 
 Peer-review time donated in 2020 
 > 100 M h 
 more than 15,000 years of work, unpaid 
 Aczel et al. 2021 [4] 
 Each value is the cited source's; bars are to scale within each card, not across cards. 
 From publication to checkable evidence 
 01 Identify DOI · authors · version 
 02 Execute Data · code · environment 
 03 Compare Expected result · tolerance 
 04 Challenge Assumptions · limits · transfer 
 Proposed methodological diagram: this workflow organizes evidence; it does not certify a study. 
 Reproducing a number does not prove that the model describes the world correctly. These levels answer different questions: documenting them separately avoids turning a badge or a repository into a blanket guarantee. 
 Documented state What is known Open question 
 Accessible A reader can obtain the materials. Does the computation run? 
 Executable The code runs in a described environment. Does it recover the reported results? 
 Reproduced A documented run recovers a result within a stated tolerance. Are the assumptions and method appropriate? 
 Validated for a use Scientific criteria and a domain of application have been examined. What happens outside that domain? 
 Connect practices without confusing their purposes 
 FAIR supports discovery and reuse; licences define permissions; reproducibility lets others check a computation; the AI Act regulates specified AI uses. RTVACOS connects this work to research excellence. These frameworks complement rather than replace one another. 
 The global picture: too many articles, too little verification 
 Output that outruns researchers. Articles indexed in Scopus and Web of Science rose by about 47% from 2016 to 2022, faster than the number of scientists; part of the growth came from special issues with shortened review times [1] . 
 A concentrated market. Five publishers published more than half of all papers as early as 2013 [2] ; the group that owns the largest reported an adjusted operating margin of 34.8% in 2025 [3] . 
 Invisible work. Reviewers gave more than 100 million hours in 2020 [4] , unpaid and almost unrecognized. 
 Eroded trust. More than 10,000 papers were retracted in 2023, over 8,000 of them in one publisher's journals, mostly in special issues exploited by paper mills [5] . 
 AI banned rather than framed. Rules say what not to do, for instance the ban on generative AI in US grant review [6] , rarely what to show. 
 What already exists 
 Level What exists What it covers 
 International FAIR principles [8] ; OSTP memo [7] Findable, reusable data; immediate access to articles and data from US federally funded research. 
 International JOSS [9] , CODECHECK [10] , ReScience C [11] , SoftwareX [20] Open software review; independent execution of an article's code; published replications; software articles and developer credit (SoftwareX). These initiatives provide different forms of review. 
 Europe Council conclusions of May 2023 [12] ; Diamond Open Access action plan [13] ; Open Research Europe [14] Immediate open access as the norm for public research; publishing at no cost to authors or readers. 
 Europe CoARA [15] Assessment reform: recognizing contributions other than article counts, peer review included. 
 Europe AI Act [16] For high-risk AI systems: data, documentation, logs, quality, post-market monitoring. 
 France Digital Republic Act, art. 30 [17] Right to post the accepted manuscript in open access after 6 months (12 in the humanities and social sciences). 
 France National Plan for Open Science [18] ; HAL; Software Heritage [19] Target of 100% open-access articles by 2030; open research source code; code archiving. 
 These texts open access . Almost none asks anyone to check that a published result can be reproduced from its data and code. 
 Who checks what? The actors, and what each mechanism is designed to cover 
 Classic peer review FAIR and repositories Licences JOSS, SoftwareX CODECHECK ReScience C AI Act (AI systems) CoARA 
 Who checks? Reviewers and journal editor Repository and data curators No one: the author declares Software-journal reviewers An independent codechecker Another team, then reviewers The provider, often by self-assessment, under market-surveillance authorities Institutions that assess 
 Text and reasoning ● · · ◐ · ◐ · · 
 Data (find, reuse) ◐ ● · · ◐ ◐ ● · 
 Reuse permissions · ◐ ● ◐ · · · · 
 Code (quality, documentation) · · · ● ◐ ◐ ● · 
 Re-running the computation · · · ◐ ● ● · · 
 Result recovered by others · · · · ◐ ● · · 
 Declared use of tools, AI included ◐ · · · · · ● · 
 Follow-up after publication ◐ ◐ · · · · ● · 
 Credit for checking work · · · · · · · ● 
 ● designed for · ◐ partly, depending on venue · · not its purpose 
 How to read: each column shows what the mechanism is for, according to its own texts, not how well it is applied. Highlighted rows have one mechanism, or none, designed for them. The AI Act covers high-risk AI systems, not articles: it is a point of comparison here. This is our reading, open to discussion row by row. 
 The AI Act as a comparison, not a regulation of papers 
 The AI Act requires providers of high-risk AI systems to govern their training, validation and test data (Art. 10), keep technical documentation (Art. 11), log events (Art. 12), run a quality management system (Art. 17) and monitor the system after it is placed on the market (Art. 72) [16] . These obligations overlap with some MLOps practices, without being equivalent. Scientific articles follow different editorial, scientific and sometimes regulatory rules; independent execution is not automatically guaranteed. 
 The regulation also excludes AI developed solely for research (Art. 2(6)). A gap may open: European teams bear the cost of compliance as soon as they deploy, teams outside the regulation do not. The AI Act remains essential all the same: it provides one framework for traceability from data to result. The right answer is not to weaken it but to bring its spirit to publishing. 
 France: editorial work that does not count 
 France has one of the most open-access-friendly legal frameworks in Europe: a mandatory right to deposit, HAL, Software Heritage, a national plan that covers source code [17] [18] . Yet editing a journal, reviewing or checking code is almost absent from career assessment, which counts articles first. The work that guarantees quality is the work that pays least; editors and reviewers become hard to find, and others end up running the reference journals. 
 What is missing 
 Checking the data and code of every article that depends on them, as the AI Act does for AI systems: frozen versions, documented environment, independent execution, kept records. 
 Declaring the tools used, AI included. Neither ban nor silence: a statement of what was used, for what, and what a human checked. 
 Following the article after publication , as one monitors a deployed system: versions, errata, reports, links to corrected datasets. 
 Recognizing editorial and review work in assessment, as CoARA proposes. 
 Connecting the frameworks : code licences, FAIR data and the AI Act talk about the same thing, traceability, but do not cite each other. 
 This is not necessarily about more journals, but about changing what we ask of the existing ones. On this site, every study links to its code and data; the page AI in research shows how to declare tools, the page Data how to choose a license, the page Cite and reuse how to give credit. 
 No verification, no trust 
 An article no one can redo is a claim, not a result. The tools to check exist, AI included; what is missing is making them normal, and recognizing the people who do that work. 
 Glossary 
 Diamond open access 
 Journals free for both authors and readers, funded by institutions. 
 APC (Article Processing Charge) 
 Fee paid by authors, or their institution, to publish an article in open access. 
 CODECHECK 
 A third party runs an article's code and certifies that the reported figures and tables are regenerated; it does not judge scientific validity. 
 CoARA 
 European coalition to reform research assessment: recognize the diversity of contributions, not only article counts. 
 DOI 
 Persistent identifier of an article, a dataset or a software version. 
 Paper mill 
 Organization selling fabricated or falsified articles, often slipped into special issues. 
 FAIR 
 Findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable: principles for data, not a license. 
 MLOps 
 Engineering practices to version, trace, deploy and monitor learning models. 
 Reproducibility 
 Recovering a result with the same data and code; replication recovers it with new data. 
 Retraction 
 Official withdrawal of a published article for serious error or fraud; the article stays visible, marked as retracted. 
 Questions and answers 
 Is scientific publishing really in trouble? 
 The number of indexed articles grew by about 47% between 2016 and 2022, faster than the number of researchers; unpaid peer review no longer keeps up, and more than 10,000 papers were retracted in 2023, a record. 
 Should AI be banned from writing and reviewing? 
 No: it should be declared. As with any other tool, authors state what was used and for what; what matters is that results are checked, data and code included. 
 Why bring the AI Act into a discussion of articles? 
 Because it requires of high-risk AI systems what articles lack: data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, a quality management system and post-market monitoring. 
 Do we need new journals? 
 Not necessarily. What is missing is verification and recognition of editorial work, not more titles.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/ai-in-research/

AI in research: the AI Act, a lab charter and a toolbox for researchers 
 Step of the story · Demonstrate trust The approach Judge against a reference, publish code, data and limits, make research findable and reusable. Principle 5: Trust is demonstrated. 
 Generative AI now writes code, drafts papers and reviews data in every laboratory. The European AI Act sets rules for what we build and what we transfer. Here is what changes for researchers, the timeline in Europe and in France, how the rest of the world compares, who is responsible when research code becomes a product, and a toolbox a lab can adopt in a few hours per project. 
 Cyril Voyant , Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E. · status on 23 October 2026 · not legal advice: check with your institution's legal service 
 In brief 
 Two research exclusions, not one: systems developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research (art. 2(6)), and research, testing and development before placing on the market , except testing in real-world conditions (art. 2(8)). The rules start when a model is placed on the market or put into service , for example when a partner deploys it in an energy system. It is high-risk when it serves as a safety component in the supply of electricity, gas or heating (Annex III, point 2); otherwise its class must be assessed case by case. 
 The deadlines moved in 2026: transparency rules apply since 2 August 2026 , high-risk systems of Annex III from 2 December 2027 , AI in regulated products from 2 August 2028 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). 
 A lab does not need a compliance department: a one-page charter , a data card and a model card , a minimal test plan and six extra fields in the data management plan give a project a documentation base that an audit can examine. The durations given below are indicative; none of this guarantees compliance. 
 What AI changes in research 
 AI speeds up what used to take days: writing code, summarizing literature, cleaning data, drafting text. It also creates new risks for science itself: invented references, fluent but wrong code, papers produced at industrial scale, models nobody can reproduce, and results that depend on a tool whose version changes without notice. The answer is the same as for any scientific tool: say what was used, check it, document it, and make it reproducible . Trust is not claimed, it is demonstrated (see questioning how we do research ). 
 The AI Act in plain words 
 One logic: the risk of the use. Some uses are banned (manipulation, social scoring), some are high-risk and strictly regulated (safety components of critical infrastructure such as electricity, gas or heating supply, medical devices, education, employment), some carry transparency duties (chatbots, synthetic content), and the rest is free. 
 Two main roles. The provider develops a system and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name (art. 3(3), 16). The deployer uses it under its authority (art. 26). Anyone who puts their name on a system, substantially modifies it or changes its purpose can become the provider (art. 25). 
 Research is excluded, under conditions. Systems and models developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research are outside the Act (art. 2(6)), and so are research, testing and development before placing on the market, except tests in real-world conditions (art. 2(8)). Free and open-source components are largely exempt unless they are high-risk, banned, or subject to transparency duties (art. 2(12)). 
 Generative AI. The obligations of August 2025 bind the providers of general-purpose models (OpenAI, Mistral, Google...), not the researchers who use them. Labeling synthetic content (art. 50) mainly binds providers and, for published deepfakes or texts informing the public without human editorial control, deployers. Declaring AI use in a paper or a thesis is required by publishers, funders and research-integrity rules (no AI as an author, disclosure of use), more than by the Act itself. 
 AI literacy (art. 4). Organizations that provide or deploy AI systems take measures so that their staff understand them; the 2026 amendment softened this into a duty of means, with support from the Commission and Member States. 
 The timeline in Europe and in France 
 Date 
 What applies 
 1 August 2024 
 The AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) enters into force 
 2 February 2025 
 Banned practices; AI literacy 
 2 August 2025 
 Obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models; governance; penalties 
 27 July 2026 
 Digital omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) in force: high-risk deadlines postponed 
 2 August 2026 
 Transparency obligations (art. 50) and most other provisions; national market surveillance 
 2 December 2026 
 End of the grace period for marking synthetic content of systems already on the market (art. 50(2)) 
 9 December 2026 
 New Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853: software is a product 
 2 December 2027 
 High-risk systems of Annex III (safety components of critical infrastructure, education, employment...) 
 2 August 2028 
 High-risk AI embedded in regulated products (Annex I: machinery, medical devices...) 
 In France , a bill adapting national law to EU law (adopted by the Senate on 18 February 2026, examined by the National Assembly in autumn 2026) organizes supervision: the DGCCRF as coordinator and single point of contact, the CNIL for banned practices and part of the high-risk uses, Arcom for synthetic content, the ACPR for finance, with technical support from ANSSI and PEReN. Until the law is passed, the European rules apply directly; the designation of authorities is what remains to be settled. 
 Elsewhere: no equivalent of the AI Act, but rules everywhere 
 Region 
 Approach (October 2026) 
 United States 
 No federal AI law. A December 2025 executive order pushes for a national framework that would override state laws, but Congress has not passed it. State laws apply: California (frontier model transparency) and Texas since January 2026, Colorado from January 2027. 
 China 
 Rules by use case: generative AI services (2023), algorithm filing, mandatory labeling of AI-generated content since 1 September 2025, enforced by the Cyberspace Administration. 
 South Korea 
 The closest equivalent: a horizontal AI Basic Act in force since 22 January 2026 (high-impact AI, transparency, local representative for foreign firms), with a one-year grace period on fines. 
 Japan 
 AI Promotion Act (2025): a framework to promote and coordinate, without penalties; guidelines for businesses. 
 Canada, Brazil 
 Canada's federal AI bill lapsed in 2025; Brazil's bill, close to the European model, passed the Senate in December 2024 and was still before the Chamber at our last check. 
 What it means for a European lab: partners abroad work under different, often lighter rules, but the AI Act reaches any system whose output is used in the EU (art. 2(1)). A shared framework is what makes collaboration safe: without it, nobody knows who answers for a model once it leaves the lab. 
 Who is responsible when research code becomes a product? 
 A model written by three labs, one of them an Asian partner, shared under a license and a consortium agreement; an EU industrial company integrates it into an energy management system and becomes its provider; the grid operator deploys it; the partner deploys it in its own country under local law; civil liability and contracts cover the whole chain 
 A typical case: a forecasting model written in part by three laboratories, one in France, one elsewhere in the EU and one at an Asian partner, within a joint project. An industrial company reuses the code in an energy management system sold in Europe. 
 While the code serves research , the three labs are outside the AI Act. They remain answerable for scientific integrity, for the documentation they deliver and for the terms of the license and the consortium agreement. 
 When the company puts the system into service under its name , it becomes the provider : if the system is a safety component of the electricity supply, it is high-risk (Annex III, point 2, from 2 December 2027): risk management, technical file, conformity assessment and CE marking. The grid operator that uses it is the deployer : human oversight, monitoring, logs. 
 If the partner deploys the model in its own country , local law applies (for example the Korean Basic Act or the Chinese labeling rules); the AI Act applies only if the output is used in the EU. 
 Civil liability follows the new Product Liability Directive from 9 December 2026: software counts as a product, but free and open-source software supplied outside a commercial activity is excluded. Everything else is settled by contracts : who may reuse the code, for what purpose, with which warranties and which duty to inform. 
 The practical lesson: write the transfer into the contract before the code leaves the lab , and hand over a documented, tested model. A model without documentation leaves its new owner with a risk nobody can measure. 
 Who is responsible? A one-minute orientation 
 Answer a few questions about one AI system. The answers point to the articles of the AI Act that apply; they are an orientation, not legal advice. 
 JavaScript is needed for this orientation. What a lab can do: the example of the O.I.E. framework 
 At the Centre O.I.E. (Mines Paris – PSL, about 30 people), a FAIR + AI framework has been drafted since 2025 and is being finalized, for deployment from 2027. Its main lines: 
 A one-page charter signed by every member : generative AI allowed as an assistant for writing, code and figures, with explicit mention of its use; human review of everything it produces; minimal documentation ( data card , model card , versioned Git repository with README); every AI project in a register , reassessed when it moves from research to industry; a data management plan with six AI fields . 
 Light roles, about 0.3 full-time equivalent in total : an AI compliance lead (register, regulatory watch, partners), a FAIR data steward (data management plans, data cards, licences, GDPR ) and an MLOps and quality referent (model cards, test plans, drift), plus an ethics committee of four people meeting each quarter for sensitive projects. 
 Six steps per project (indicative durations): register (5 minutes); data management plan with AI fields (1 hour); data card and model card (2 hours); minimal test plan (2 to 3 hours); README with the AI-use statement (30 minutes); for a transfer, an audit-ready file (one day). 
 Indicators : at least 95 % of projects documented, less than five days between project start and an enriched plan, partner satisfaction above 8/10. 
 At the institution level, Mines Paris – PSL's legal service has built, with the research centers, a self-assessment decision tree : who is the actor and in which role, the essential questions, the impacts, the qualification of the AI system in the risk pyramid, the conditions of use and of making it available. Its purpose is to find the tipping point where a project enters the scope of the AI Act, and to adapt the contract and its technical annex in time. It is a good example of what an institution can offer its researchers. 
 The toolbox 
 Each tool opens on a filled example, taken from the O.I.E. templates (values marked illustrative are not results). Download the nine templates as a kit (Markdown files in a zip, ready to fill in). 
 1. Situate the project. Research only, transfer, or deployment? Who will be provider and deployer? Which risk class? Real-world tests are not covered by the research exemption. 
 2. State the use of AI. In a paper, a thesis, a report or a README: which tool, which version, for what, checked by whom and when. Example: "Parts of the data-loading code were drafted with GitHub Copilot (2026); all functions were reviewed and unit-tested by A. Author on 12 March 2026." 
 Example: README with the AI-use statement 
 Project: MLP, global horizontal irradiance (GHI) forecasting · Author: First Last · Supervisor: First Last · O.I.E., Mines Paris – PSL 
 Purpose : train a multilayer perceptron to forecast hourly GHI from weather data. 
 Use of AI : occasional help from a generative AI assistant (name and version) for boilerplate code and debugging. Every suggestion was reviewed by the author (unit tests, validation by the supervisor), name and date. 
 Data : SIAR network (Spain), 2005–2015; normalization, gap handling; public, non-personal data; license stated. 
 Tests : fixed seed, identical results on repeated runs; cross-validation (k > 3 folds); stress test on irradiance peaks and missing values; drift checked with nRMSE and NICE on recent data. 
 Reuse : academic research; any industrial use must be agreed with the laboratory. 
 3. Keep a human in charge. No AI as an author; every reference, equation and line of code checked by a named person. 
 4. Document the data ( data card ). Origin, period, volume, variables and units, preprocessing, quality, known biases, license or legal basis, transfers outside the EU, conditions of reuse. 
 Example: data card (one page)

 5. Document the model ( model card ). Name and version, architecture, training and test data with the split, intended use, metrics against an explicit reference (persistence, for example with NICE metrics ), limits, human oversight, link to the code version.

 6. Test before sharing. Reproducibility (fixed seed, same results), robustness (cross-validation, subsamples), stress tests (extreme or missing values), drift on recent data. 
 Example: minimal test plan (checklist, half a day) 
 Test 
 How 
 Why 
 Who validates 
 Reproducibility 
 Fixed seed, identical results; hash of weights and dataset 
 A third party can reproduce the results

 The model does not overfit one dataset

 Extreme data: irradiance peaks, gaps, sensor anomalies

 Responsible supervisor 
 For a model in operation, a monitoring plan adds thresholds, for example: nRMSE checked monthly, alert above +0.05 and critical above +0.10, then analysis and retraining; data coverage checked weekly, alert below 95 %; more than three incidents a month triggers an urgent diagnosis. 
 7. Add six fields to the data management plan . Legal basis; human oversight; AI transparency; conditions of reuse; international transfers; impact assessment ( DPIA where personal-data processing is likely to create a high risk to people, FRIA for some high-risk deployments). 
 Example: the six AI fields of a data management plan 
 Legal basis : for personal data, identify the applicable basis under Article 6 GDPR , and Article 9 conditions where relevant. Record copyright licences and reuse agreements separately; they do not replace a GDPR legal basis. 
 Human oversight : who validates the results, when, at which level (in, on or outside the loop). 
 AI transparency : whether content or code was generated with AI, and how it is stated. 
 Conditions of reuse : free, under license, or reserved to a contract. 
 International transfers : whether data leave the EU (non-European cloud, partner abroad) and the safeguards. 
 Impact assessment : DPIA where personal-data processing is likely to create a high risk to people; FRIA for some high-risk public deployments; otherwise, why neither applies. 
 Example: DPIA and FRIA screening, two contrasting projects 
 Document the decision and its justification; a numerical score does not determine a legal obligation. DPIA : the controller assesses whether personal-data processing is likely to pose a high risk, with advice from the DPO where designated ( CNIL ). FRIA : check the intended use, high-risk classification and deployer against Article 27 ; Annex III point 2 is excluded from this specific obligation. 
 Weather-only forecasting for a thesis : in this stated scenario, no personal-data processing requiring a DPIA is identified. Record the research context and check applicability again before deployment. 
 Household load forecasting for a grid operator : assess the privacy risks of consumption profiles with the controller and DPO. Do not infer a FRIA obligation from the energy sector alone. Document the intended use, applicable category and responsible parties; an assessment can also be undertaken voluntarily. 
 8. Keep a register of AI projects, uses and partners, and reassess when a project changes purpose. 
 Example: one line of the AI register 
 Project 
 Model 
 Use of generative AI 
 Status 
 Partners 
 Data 
 Last review 
 GHI forecasting, thesis 2026

 Code assistant, stated in README 
 Research only 
 None 
 Public weather data 
 Project start; on any change of purpose 
 9. Before any transfer, write the contract and prepare the file. Who becomes provider; license and intellectual property; warranties and liability; duty to report incidents; data transfers; the technical file (README, data card, model card, test plan and results, change log, monitoring plan). 
 Example: content of an audit-ready file 
 README with the use of generative AI and the licences of data and code; 
 data card (origin, biases, legal basis, reuse) and model card (type, data, metrics, limits, human oversight, Git traceability); 
 test plan and its results, validated by the supervisor; 
 data management plan with the six AI fields; 
 change log: versions of the model, Git commits, changes of the dataset; 
 for a high-risk deployment: monitoring plan (nRMSE, NICE, drift, thresholds) and an incident procedure (reporting channel, named person, time to fix). 
 10. Train everyone. A short session for PhD students and staff each year covers AI literacy and the lab's charter . 
 Example: a one-page laboratory charter 
 As a member of the laboratory, I commit to the following principles for using and developing artificial intelligence, in line with the AI Act and the FAIR principles. 
 Generative AI (chat assistants, code assistants) is allowed as an aid for writing, code and figures, and its use is always stated (report, paper, README). 
 Human review : everything produced with AI is checked by a person; technical and bibliographic review before any release. The author remains responsible. 
 Minimal documentation for every project: a data card, a model card, a versioned Git repository with a README (the institution's platform; projects may stay private). 
 AI register : every project using AI is listed; moving from research to industry triggers a new assessment. 
 Data management plan with the six AI fields: legal basis, human oversight, AI transparency, reuse, international transfers, impact assessment. 
 Name, role, date, signature. 
 Glossary 
 GDPR 
 General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679: the European law on personal data. See the CNIL guide . 
 DPIA 
 Data Protection Impact Assessment (art. 35 GDPR): required when processing personal data is likely to result in a high risk for people. CNIL method and tool . 
 FRIA 
 Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (art. 27 AI Act): required from some deployers of high-risk AI systems, mainly public bodies and private entities providing public services, before first use. 
 MLOps 
 Machine-learning operations: the practices that keep a model reproducible and reliable once in use: versioning of data and code, automated tests, monitoring of performance and drift, controlled retraining. 
 Data management plan (DMP) 
 A document describing how a project collects, documents, stores, shares and archives its data, required by ANR and Horizon Europe; written in France with DMP OPIDoR . 
 Data card, model card 
 One- to two-page sheets that describe a dataset or a trained model: origin, content, intended use, metrics, limits. The format follows the "model cards" and "datasheets for datasets" proposals of the machine-learning community. 
 Official resources 
 AI Act: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on EUR-Lex and the European Commission's AI policy page 
 European Commission: living guidelines on the responsible use of generative AI in research 
 CNIL: AI and personal data and the DPIA guide 
 Data management plans: DMP OPIDoR 
 Standards: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (AI management system) and ISO/IEC 23894:2023 (AI risk management) 
 Publishing ethics: COPE position on authorship and AI tools 
 Limits 
 This page summarizes public texts and the work of one laboratory; it is not legal advice. National laws, guidance and standards are still moving: dates are given as checked on 23 October 2026. For a real project, ask your institution's legal service.

 The approach: AI in its place, trust demonstrated 
 Frequently asked questions 
 Is scientific research exempt from the AI Act? 
 The exclusions depend on the system's purpose and stage, not simply on the user's status as a researcher. Article 2 covers systems specifically developed and put into service solely for scientific research, and certain pre-market research activities. Real-world testing is outside the latter exclusion. Reassess the scope before transfer or deployment. 
 Official source 
 Which high-risk AI deadlines should a laboratory track? 
 As checked on October 23, 2026, the revised timeline provides December 2, 2027 for Annex III high-risk uses and August 2, 2028 for high-risk AI embedded in regulated products under Annex I. Other obligations have their own dates. Identify the relevant system and provision before applying a deadline. 
 Official source 
 Who is responsible when laboratory code is transferred? 
 Identify the provider, deployer and other actors for the actual system. For high-risk systems, Article 25 specifies circumstances in which rebranding, substantial modification or a changed intended purpose can make another actor the provider. Contracts should document roles; they do not replace the applicable statutory obligations. 
 Official source 
 What should a laboratory document first? 
 Record the purpose, people responsible, data provenance, model and code versions, validation results and limits. Use data and model cards, an AI-use statement and a project register. Before a transfer, review roles and documentation with the institution's legal service. These are practical recommendations, not a compliance certification. 
 Read also: Scientific publishing: no verification of data and code, no trust

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/data/

Models live in the data: qualify, certify, license 
 With AI, anyone writes a forecasting model or a neural network in minutes. The method is no longer scarce; the data are . A model learns only what its data contain: if they are wrong, shifted in time or of unknown origin, so is the model, confidently. Data must therefore be qualified, certified and licensed before anything learns from them. 
 The basic rules 
 Findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable (FAIR principles), from acquisition onwards, not at the end of a project. 
 Described : standard metadata (origin, instrument, units, time step, time zone, processing). 
 Qualified : a written, traced quality control (physical bounds, stuck values, timestamps, comparison with a reference), whose result travels with the data. 
 Identified : a persistent identifier (DOI) per dataset and per version. 
 In open formats and services (NetCDF-CF, OGC standards) rather than isolated files. 
 Under an explicit license : without one, nobody knows what they may do. 
 An example: Webservice-Energy 
 Webservice-Energy is the spatial data infrastructure of the O.I.E. centre (Observation, Impacts, Energy) of Mines Paris – PSL , developed and operated for almost twenty years for energy, the environment and Earth observation, "FAIR by design". Its main architects are Lionel Ménard ( ORCID ) and Raphaël Jolivet (contact: lionel.menard@minesparis.psl.eu , raphael.jolivet@minesparis.psl.eu ). 
 Find : a metadata catalogue ( GeoNetwork , ISO 19115/19139, INSPIRE , OGC ) for data, services, publications and software. 
 Access : a THREDDS server ( OPeNDAP , NetCDF Subset Service, WMS), OGC map services (WMS, WFS, WCS), remote processing (WPS) and a STAC catalog under development. 
 Harmonize ground measurements : the open library libinsitu brings heterogeneous networks to the same NetCDF-CF format, with their quality control. 
 Identify and license : DOIs assigned to datasets through DataCite , and a CC BY license. 
 Connect : community portal of the Group on Earth Observations (GEO) , Copernicus data ( CAMS for the atmosphere, C3S for the climate), Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe projects. 
 Choosing a license for code and data 
 After the reflection led at the O.I.E. center by Raphaël Jolivet . The usual practice is binary: close everything when commercial valorization is hoped for, open everything (CC BY, MIT, Apache, BSD) otherwise. It rests on an estimate made too early, and it limits the diffusion of the very work one wants to protect, while diffusion is often what creates opportunities. A middle way exists: non-commercial licences (CC BY-NC for data, PolyForm Noncommercial for code). They are not "open source" in the OSI sense, but they remain compatible with academic open access and reproducibility, and keep a future valorization possible. 
 The tree below is an example, nothing fixed : each research center adapts it to its contracts, its partners and its institution's policy. 
 Which license? The decision tree 
 First: the agreement of every rights holder. 
 JavaScript is needed for this tree. An example. A forecasting code developed on own funds, with no diffusion constraint, an industrial potential and no GPL dependency: "no" to confidentiality, "no" to imposed openness, "no" to a software journal, hence a non-commercial license . The same code published in SoftwareX would go under an open-source license. 
 An orientation, not legal advice: the institution's policy and the contracts prevail. To cite or reuse our work: Cite and reuse . 
 Glossary 
 FAIR 
 Findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable: four principles so that data serve beyond those who produced them. 
 Metadata 
 Data about the data: origin, instrument, units, period, time step, processing, license. 
 DOI 
 A persistent identifier for a digital object (article, dataset, software); the address remains valid even if the website changes. DataCite assigns them to research data. 
 OGC 
 Open Geospatial Consortium: open standards for geographic services, among them WMS (maps), WFS (features), WCS (grids) and WPS (remote processing). 
 INSPIRE, ISO 19115 
 The European directive on geographic information and the international standard for its metadata. 
 THREDDS, OPeNDAP 
 A scientific data server and the protocol that reads only the useful part (an area, a period) without downloading everything. 
 NetCDF-CF 
 A file format for scientific grids and series, with conventions (CF) that fix variable names, units and coordinates. 
 STAC 
 SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog: a standard way to catalog satellite imagery and cloud-native data. 
 GEO, Copernicus, CAMS, C3S 
 The Group on Earth Observations (an intergovernmental partnership), the European Earth observation program and two of its services: atmosphere (CAMS) and climate change (C3S). 
 CC BY 
 Creative Commons Attribution: anyone may copy, adapt and reuse, commercially too, provided the author is credited. Meant for texts, figures and data. 
 CC BY-NC 
 The same, for non-commercial uses only. 
 MIT 
 A very permissive software license: free use, modification, redistribution and sale, provided the copyright notice and the license text are kept; no warranty. 
 Apache 2.0 
 Permissive like MIT, plus an explicit patent license from contributors and a duty to flag modified files. 
 BSD 
 A family of permissive licences close to MIT; the three-clause version also forbids using the authors' names to promote a derived product. 
 GPL 
 A copyleft license: any derived software that is distributed must be under the GPL, with its source code. 
 PolyForm Noncommercial 
 A software license that allows any non-commercial use: personal use, research, experiment, teaching, and use by non-commercial organizations (educational institutions, public research, charities, government bodies). Commercial use needs another agreement with the author. The license must travel with redistributed code. 
 Open source (OSI) 
 The Open Source Initiative definition: an open-source license may not restrict any field of use; a non-commercial license is therefore not "open source", even if the code is open to read. 
 Read also: Scientific publishing: no verification of data and code, no trust

 Everything published here may be reused. The only request: credit the authors and their laboratory , the O.I.E. center (Observation, Impacts, Energy) of Mines Paris – PSL, and link to the source.

 Articles The journal's (often CC BY when open access) The full reference with every co-author and the DOI; the list is on the news page , ORCID and HAL . 
 Software The repository's ( LICENSE file: MIT, BSD, GPL…) The repository's "all versions" Zenodo DOI, or GitHub's "Cite this repository" button ( CITATION.cff ), plus the associated article when there is one.

Collaborate 
 Collaborate: research projects, studies and adaptation of the tools 
 Your question, a method you can check, a result you can defend. 
 Everything on these sites is open: the theory, the code, the limits. The next step is your data and your decision. Bring a real problem; we start from what is known about the system, beat an explicit reference, and add complexity only where it pays. 
 Write to me Explore the methods and code Three ways to work together 
 1 Answer a call for projects 
 National (ANR, ADEME), European (Horizon Europe) or regional calls, as partner or coordinator: energy forecasting, renewables on the grid, evaluation of models, medical physics, responsible AI in research. 
 2 Fund it directly with the school 
 A collaborative research contract: a study, an internship, a co-supervised doctorate (for example under the French CIFRE scheme) or a postdoctoral project. 
 3 Explore a research direction together 
 An academic collaboration to explore a research question together, compare approaches or open a new scientific direction. Each team’s objectives and contributions are defined from the outset, with a view to sharing or applying the work: a joint paper, open software, a dataset or transfer to practice. 
 Collaborations that became results 
 Medicine With Marie Fusella Giuntini, Dominique Barbolosi and David Taieb: three equations calibrated on 50 patients to explore radioiodine protocols before treating anyone ( Scientific Reports , 2026). 
 Read the story → 
 Research on research With John P. A. Ioannidis (Stanford University), Jeroen Baas and Roy Boverhof (Elsevier): a science-wide map of institutions, impact next to integrity ( Royal Society Open Science , 2026). 
 Read the story → 
 Energy With Andreas Kazantzidis (University of Patras) and Jan Kleissl (UC San Diego): does a satellite forecast need the whole field, or one cell? Open code and data, manuscript in preparation. 
 Read the story → 
 What can be adapted to your data 
 Forecast evaluation : NICE metrics , γ-index for forecast fields. 
 Reference forecasts : BLEND and CLIPER , ARTU , variability and forecastability with sCV and F . 
 Frugal learning : MIMO-ELM for an energy mix, satellite irradiance forecasting. 
 Medical physics : LQL-Equiv for dose equivalence, the radioiodine therapy model . 
 Simulation and AI in practice : road tunnel loads , WebSemantic (a language model reads, validated code computes). 
 How it works 
 Write a short email: the question, the data, the decision it serves, the timeline. 
 A first exchange frames the problem: what is known about the system, which reference to beat, what precision is really needed. 
 Academic exploration develops directly between researchers. Depending on the project, a research contract or a service agreement (testing, targeted analysis) may be established. Where needed, the relevant departments at Mines Paris – PSL define the terms for intellectual property, confidentiality and publication. 
 Once the framework is agreed, we define a clear research plan: objectives, methods, data, staffing and technical resources, milestones, schedule and deliverables. Evaluation criteria and decision points are set from the outset to track progress and make evidence-based adjustments. Results are shared under the terms of the agreement. 
 A question and some data? Let's look at it together. 
 Exploratory exchanges between researchers can begin directly. Research contracts and service agreements are established with Mines Paris – PSL. 
 Name Organization Your email Kind of collaboration Your question, your data and your timeline Your message is delivered to cyril.voyant@minesparis.psl.eu through FormSubmit (formsubmit.co), a form-delivery service. Your details are used only to answer you; this site keeps nothing. 
 cyril.voyant@minesparis.psl.eu

The RTVACOS tree: where can your work break? 
 Research has an effect only if it is found, judged credible and reused. The RTVACOS framework describes this as a multiplicative system: four foundations, where a single weakness drags everything down, and three amplifiers, which scale a solid base but never replace it. 
 Tick what your project already does. Roots are foundations, branches are amplifiers. A bare root turns the whole tree pale: that is the multiplicative logic. 
 R · Rigour (foundation) A simple reference to beat (persistence, climatology…) Separate training and test data, without leakage Limits and domain of validity written down T · Transparency (foundation) Public code, with a license Data or their access described, with a license Tool use declared, AI included V · Visibility (foundation) An ORCID and DOIs (article, code, data) A clear page: the result, the method, how to cite Machine-readable metadata (CITATION.cff, JSON-LD) A · Adoption (foundation) An example that runs in minutes Documentation for a user who is not the author Real user feedback taken into account C · Collaboration (amplifier) Co-authors who strengthen a foundation, not only the list Credited contributions (CRediT, ORCID) O · Outreach (amplifier) A summary for non-specialists A talk, a course or a video S · Societal relevance (amplifier) An identified user or decision A partner outside academia A mirror for reflection, not a scoring instrument: the authors claim no empirical validation and discuss limits themselves, such as the risk of gamification and the unequal distribution of skills. 
 The framework 
 Cyril Voyant , Rodrigo Amaro e Silva , Nicolas Fichaux , Lionel Ménard , Sylvain Cros , Rodanthi-Elisavet Mamouri . Beyond Publish and Pray: Engineering Research Excellence . SSRN, 2026. 
 The talk (45 min) and its questions 
 Scientific publishing: no verification, no trust

Teaching 
 Five courses, open to all under CC BY 4.0, from health studies to energy. The same habit runs through them: start from the signal or the data, compare with a simple reference, measure what a model adds. 
 Open courses 
 Most courses are in French; the English guide to the open courses describes each one, chapter by chapter. 
 Forecasting the intermittent solar resource 
 Mines Paris – PSL engineering curriculum, applied research project UE14 · 59 slides · English and French · CC BY 4.0 
 How to forecast solar irradiance one hour ahead, on ten years of real measurements from Ajaccio, adding complexity only where it pays. 
 The solar signal: geometry, clear sky and the clear-sky index (an additive deviation), what can and cannot be predicted. 
 The data: ten years of hourly measurements, quality control, day and night. 
 The references to beat: simple persistence, smart persistence, climatology. 
 Autoregressive models fitted by least squares, the model order, the sliding window. 
 Extreme Learning Machines: principle, number of neurons, the risk of overfitting. 
 Evaluation: nRMSE, nMAE, skill, NICE; test on the year 2007, daytime and day and night. 
 Online learning and frugality: how much model is really needed? 
 Open the course → 
 Archived and citable on Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23620102 
 Biostatistics for health studies (in French) 
 First-year health studies (PASS, UE8) · 3 chapters, 246 slides · in French · CC BY 4.0 
 The statistical tools a future health professional needs to read a study, interpret a test and decide with data. 
 Why statistics in health: variability, therapeutic adjustment, correlation and causation, hidden variables. 
 Probabilities: random experiments, events, counting, conditional probabilities, the Bayesian approach. 
 Diagnostic tests: contingency tables, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, ROC curves. 
 Descriptive statistics: measurement scales, graphs, central tendency, dispersion, skewness. 
 The normal distribution: standardization, the z table, intervals. 
 Hypothesis tests: null and alternative hypotheses, risks, comparison of means. 
 Pearson correlation, linear regression, coefficient of determination and significance. 
 χ² goodness-of-fit and independence tests, with exercises. 
 Open the course (in French) → 
 Physics for health studies: electromagnetic waves, X-rays and imaging (in French) 
 First-year health studies (PASS-PACES), physical bases of medical imaging · 110-slide lecture and 2 corrected exercise sessions · in French · CC BY 4.0 
 The physical bases of medical imaging, from the wave to the CT scanner. 
 The nature of electromagnetic waves: speed, sinusoidal wave, wave vector. 
 Wave-particle duality: photon energy E = hν, the electronvolt. 
 The electromagnetic spectrum and its energy ranges. 
 The energy levels of the atom and the case of hydrogen. 
 Absorption, emission, fluorescence, Auger effect, spectroscopy; an application: pulse oximetry. 
 X-rays: the Coolidge tube, bremsstrahlung and fluorescence radiation, spectrum, radiation protection. 
 Photon-matter interactions: photoelectric effect, Compton effect, pair production, attenuation and half-value layer. 
 Imaging: contrast, conventional radiography, CT scanning and windowing.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/stories/lql-equiv/

Compute, don't learn: radiobiological dose equivalence with LQL-Equiv 
 Step of the story · Compute directly The approach When the link is known, compute it with an explicit model, calibrated and validated on data; learning is added only for a demonstrated benefit. Principle 2: The model at the core. 
 When the link between a radiotherapy schedule and its biological effect is known, it is computed directly. No data and no artificial intelligence are needed: only a model we understand, checked case by case. 
 Cyril Voyant , with Daniel Julian · Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E. 
 In brief 
 One fraction of 15 Gy to the rectum has a biologically effective dose of 72.7 Gy under the linear-quadratic (LQ) model, but 59.4 Gy under the linear-quadratic-linear (LQL) model: 18 % lower . 
 LQL-Equiv computes these equivalences directly from an explicit model. Its 2026 version reproduces the 2014 software on 4,438 treatment schedules (69,125 of 69,131 values agree, 99.991 %). 
 It is a research and teaching tool, not a medical device . 
 The finding 
 The answer to "are these two schedules equivalent?" does not need to be learned from data: it follows from a radiobiological model whose parameters are documented. Computing it directly is exact, explainable and reproducible, and the choice of model matters: at high doses per fraction, LQ and LQL differ by tens of grays. 
 The question 
 Two treatments can deliver the same total dose very differently: 39 fractions of 2 Gy, or 5 fractions of 7 Gy. Are they equivalent for the tumour, and for the healthy organs around it? Radiotherapy answers with the biologically effective dose (BED) and its translation into a dose given in 2 Gy fractions ( EQD2 ). 
 The theory, in plain words 
 For n fractions of dose d , the linear-quadratic model gives 
 BED = n · d · (1 + d / (α/β)) 
 where α/β describes how sensitive a tissue is to the size of each fraction (about 3.9 Gy for the rectum). The term d/(α/β) is why large fractions count for more than their dose. The equivalent dose in 2 Gy fractions is then EQD2 = BED / (1 + 2/(α/β)) . 
 The LQ curve keeps bending upward as the dose per fraction grows, which overstates the effect of very large fractions. The LQL model keeps the LQ curve up to a transition dose d_T (7.8 Gy for the rectum) and continues it as a straight line beyond. LQL-Equiv also handles gaps, two fractions a day and tumour repopulation; the full equations are on the technical page. 
 Where it sits on the complexity ladder 
 Complexity ladder: LQL-Equiv stops at the first rung, direct calculation 
 First rung: direct calculation . The link between inputs and outputs is known, so climbing further, to statistics or machine learning, would add data needs and uncertainty without adding anything. AI belongs in every toolbox, not in every solution. 
 The example in figures 
 BED per fraction for the rectum, LQ and LQL 
 One fraction of 15 Gy to the rectum: 
 LQ: 15 × (1 + 15/3.9) = 72.7 Gy ; 
 LQL: 7.8 × (1 + 7.8/3.9) + 5 × (15 − 7.8) = 23.4 + 36.0 = 59.4 Gy . 
 The gap grows with the dose per fraction. This is why the choice of model must be stated when hypofractionated and conventional schedules are compared. The calculator then adds the time and repair corrections of each tissue. 
 What it brings, and its limits 
 Brings : a transparent calculation, documented parameters for 34 organs at risk and 20 tumour sites, case-by-case validation against the original software, and a free calculator that runs in the browser (nothing entered leaves the page). 
 Limits : the result is only as good as the model and its parameters (α/β, d_T, slope of the linear tail), which remain uncertain. Complication and control probabilities (NTCP, TCP) are model illustrations, never validated against clinical outcomes. Not for choosing or changing a prescription. 
 Two companion articles go further: a comparison of LQ and LQL for clinical decision-making ( Clinical Oncology , 2025), and a call for standardizing dose-equivalence calculations ( Medical Dosimetry , 2026). 
 Go further 
 Full theory, runnable code and validation : https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/tools/lql-equiv.html 
 The calculator : https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/LQL-Equiv-web/ 
 Articles :

 C. Voyant, D. Julian, Medical Dosimetry (2026), doi: 10.1016/j.meddos.2026.08.002 ; 
 C. Voyant, D. Julian et al., Clinical Oncology 45, 103893 (2025), doi: 10.1016/j.clon.2025.103893 ; 
 C. Voyant et al., Reports of Practical Oncology and Radiotherapy (2014), doi: 10.1016/j.rpor.2013.08.004 .

 The approach behind this work : Understand before you compute

Questioning how we do research: influence, integrity, excellence 
 Step of the story · Demonstrate trust The approach Judge against a reference, publish code, data and limits, make research findable and reusable. Principle 5: Trust is demonstrated. 
 Research in a changing world also has to examine its own methods. The same approach applies: compare with an explicit reference, look at what a single number hides, and state the limits. 
 Who did what. The science-wide map of institutions: John P. A. Ioannidis (Meta-Research Innovation Center at Stanford, Stanford University), Jeroen Baas and Roy Boverhof (Elsevier, Amsterdam), with Cyril Voyant (Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E.). The Influence Index: Cyril Voyant , Jeroen Baas , Roy Boverhof , Paolo Stringari , Mathilde Marchand-Lasserre and John P. A. Ioannidis . The excellence framework: Cyril Voyant , Rodrigo Amaro e Silva , Nicolas Fichaux , Lionel Menard , Sylvain Cros and Rodanthi-Elisavet Mamouri . 
 In brief 
 Counting highly cited researchers mixes up size and concentration. A share compared with a neutral 2 % baseline , on a doubling scale, says how concentrated influence is, independently of the size of an institution. 
 Impact alone is not enough: a science-wide map of institutions by J. P. A. Ioannidis (Stanford), J. Baas and R. Boverhof (Elsevier) and C. Voyant, in Royal Society Open Science (2026), puts it next to research-integrity proxies : retractions, extreme self-citation, publication in discontinued journals. 
 Publishing is no longer enough either: in a saturated system, research must be found, trusted and reused . The RTVACOS framework treats excellence as a multiplicative system in which one weak foundation collapses the whole. 
 The finding 
 The tools we use to judge research deserve the same scrutiny as the models we use to forecast the sun or compute a dose. A volume indicator rewards size; a single score hides integrity problems; a good paper nobody finds has no impact. Each of these questions has the same answer as elsewhere in this work: an explicit reference, several complementary measures, and stated limits. 
 The question 
 How should an institution, a funder or a researcher read research performance at a time when output has grown fourfold since 2004 and AI writing tools accelerate it further? Which indicators measure what we think they measure? 
 The theory, in plain words 
 Influence, independently of size. With X highly cited authors among N eligible authors of an institution, the share is p = X/N . It is compared with the share expected by construction of the Top 2 % lists, p₀ = 0.02 : 
 I = log₂(p / p₀) 
 I = 0 means the baseline, I = +1 twice the baseline, I = −1 half of it. The scale is symmetric and does not depend on the size of the institution or on the performance of others. The idea is the same as comparing a forecast with persistence: a score means something only against a stated reference. 
 Impact and integrity, side by side. The science-wide map published in Royal Society Open Science (2026) adds three proxies of possible integrity problems: authorships in papers retracted for reasons other than publisher errors, and the shares of top-cited authors with extreme self-citation or many publications in titles discontinued by Scopus. 
 Excellence as a system. RTVACOS treats excellence as E ∝ (R × T × V × A) × (1 + C + O + S) : four foundations (Rigour, Transparency, Visibility, Adoption) that multiply each other, so that a zero in one collapses the whole, and three amplifiers (Collaboration, Outreach, Societal relevance) that scale a solid base but cannot replace it. 
 The example in figures 
 The Influence Index on a doubling scale: 1 % gives −1, 2 % gives 0, 4 % gives +1, 8 % gives +2 
 An institution where 4 % of the eligible authors are in the Top 2 % lists has I = +1 : twice the baseline. One at 1 % has I = −1 . These shares are illustrative. 
 What it brings, and its limits 
 Brings : indicators that separate size from concentration; impact read together with integrity; open datasets that let anyone redo the analysis; a reflection framework for researchers and institutions on rigour, transparency, visibility and adoption. 
 Limits : citation-based indicators are proxies, not judgments of individuals or of quality; integrity proxies flag patterns to examine, not misconduct. RTVACOS is a heuristic for reflection, not a scoring instrument, and claims no empirical validation. The application of the Influence Index to French universities is a manuscript in submission ( Scientometrics ); its results will be reported once published. 
 Go further 
 Article : J. P. A. Ioannidis, J. Baas, R. Boverhof, C. Voyant, Science-wide mapping of institutions based on affiliated authors' impact and research integrity proxies, Royal Society Open Science 13, 260870 (2026), doi:10.1098/rsos.260870 (open access) · preprint doi:10.64898/2025.12.16.694665 · data doi:10.17632/jn5j7gjpzj.1 
 Influence Index, code and processed data : github.com/cyrilvoyant/influence-index-bibliometrics · doi:10.5281/zenodo.19706465 · manuscript A Log-Based Influence Index for Evaluating Research Institutions (C. Voyant, J. Baas, R. Boverhof, P. Stringari, M. Marchand-Lasserre, J. P. A. Ioannidis), in submission 
 Excellence framework (RTVACOS) : C. Voyant, R. Amaro e Silva, N. Fichaux, L. Menard, S. Cros, R.-E. Mamouri, Beyond Publish and Pray: Engineering Research Excellence , SSRN preprint (2026), doi:10.2139/ssrn.6877118 · the talk, summary and references 
 In French : op-ed in News Tank Éducation & Recherche (3 March 2026) and the post Excellence scientifique à l'ère de l'IA : du SEO au GEO on this site 
 The approach behind this work : Understand before you compute

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/stories/satellite-irradiance/

Satellite irradiance forecasting: one cell, a patch or the whole field 
 Step of the story · Learn frugally The approach When the useful relations are not known well enough, evaluate what the data can teach, with only as much complexity as pays. Principle 3: Complexity only if it pays. 
 A satellite sees the irradiance of a whole region every hour. It is tempting to give a forecaster the whole map. Holding the forecaster fixed and changing only what it reads shows how much of that map actually helps. 
 Cyril Voyant (Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E.), with Andreas Kazantzidis (University of Patras) and Jan Kleissl (University of California San Diego) · manuscript in preparation, open code and data extract 
 In brief 
 Every model forecasts the next 24 hourly values of one satellite cell over Corsica from its 24 past values; only what it reads changes: its own cell, a patch, the whole field, or a compressed field . 
 In the public repository, an extreme learning machine reading its own cell has the lowest pooled error ( nRMSE 0.308 ), ahead of the same model reading the whole field (0.355) with a thousand times fewer parameters , and of a U-Net (0.343) and an LSTM (0.326) reading the field. 
 It is one region, one satellite product and one two-year split: a benchmark result, not a general law . 
 The finding 
 On this record, the hourly history of the cell itself carries most of what an hour-by-hour forecast of the next day can use. Reading the rest of the map adds parameters faster than it removes error: none of the seven compression methods tested and neither of the two deep networks reading the whole field reaches the per-cell model. 
 The question 
 Satellite irradiance comes as maps. Deep networks such as U-Nets and LSTMs read whole fields; compression methods shrink the field before a model reads it. Both add inputs and parameters. How much of that spatial information lowers the error of a forecast for each of the next 24 hours, and at what cost in stored parameters? 
 The theory, in plain words 
 One forecaster, several inputs. The forecaster is an extreme learning machine (ELM): a hidden layer of neurons drawn at random and never trained, and output weights fitted in one linear least-squares solve. Training takes seconds and the number of stored parameters is easy to count. The same forecaster reads either its own cell, a 3 × 3 patch, the whole field of 722 cells, or the field compressed by one of seven methods (Radon transform, DCT, wavelets, PCA, random projection, subsampling, autoencoder). 
 Fair references. Persistence repeats the last hour, the 24-hour persistence repeats the same hour of the previous day, and BLEND mixes the two. A model is worth its parameters only if it beats them. 
 Fair scoring. Errors are pooled over all cells, all lead times from 1 to 24 hours and all test hours where the Sun is more than 5° above the horizon. The nRMSE is divided by the mean scored observation of the test year, 407.9 W/m². 
 The example in figures 
 Pooled error against parameters stored by each model (log scale): the per-cell ELM is the lowest point; reading the whole field moves models to the right without moving them down 
 The data are HelioClim-3 irradiance (Heliosat-2 method, Meteosat images, SoDa service) on 1,148 points over Corsica, hourly, with 2005 for training and 2006 for testing. 
 The per-cell ELM reaches nRMSE 0.308 with about 100 thousand stored parameters; the whole-field ELM reaches 0.355 with about 100 million. 
 In W/m²: 0.308 × 407.9 ≈ 126 W/m² against about 145 W/m² for the whole-field ELM. 
 A 3 × 3 patch does not help either (0.3087 against 0.3077 for a single cell). 
 The 24-hour persistence scores 0.396, BLEND 0.376: every learned model beats them. 
 What it brings, and its limits 
 Brings : a protocol where only the input changes, so that the value of spatial information is measured, not assumed; a parameter count next to every error, in line with the frugal approach; code that rebuilds the tables in seconds. 
 Limits : one region, one satellite product (HelioClim-3), hourly steps and a single 2005/2006 split. Intra-hour nowcasting driven by cloud motion can behave differently. The manuscript is in preparation; only the numbers of the public repository are reported here. 
 Go further 
 Full theory, equations, results table and code : the technical guide 
 Code and data extract : github.com/cyrilvoyant/cell-vs-field-irradiance · archive doi:10.5281/zenodo.23562557 · data HelioClim-3, SoDa service, under its terms of use 
 Same idea elsewhere : MIMO-ELM, seven energy signals of Corsica forecast by one model · how much model is enough?

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/stories/thyroid-radioiodine/

Thyroid cancer and radioiodine: model first, learn only what is missing 
 Step of the story · Hybridize The approach When the model falls short, complete it: keep the model, learn only what is missing. Principle 2: The model at the core. 
 How many sessions of radioactive iodine, how far apart, and at what activity? An intelligible model of three equations explores these questions before any patient is treated. Learning will be added only where the model is not enough. 
 Marie Fusella Giuntini and Dominique Barbolosi , with Cyril Voyant and David Taieb 
 In brief 
 Three equations (radioactive iodine activity, tumour cells, thyroglobulin) describe how metastatic thyroid cancer responds to radioiodine therapy; their parameters were calibrated on 50 patients . 
 The tumour doubling time separates the profiles: about 9.8 months for a refractory profile and 66.6 months for a responding one in the published demonstrators. 
 The model makes it possible to explore the number of sessions, the interval between them and the activity before treating. Learning is planned only where the model falls short, in a hybrid approach that keeps the model at its core. 
 The finding 
 The model and its simulator, RAIR-Sim, are the work of Marie Fusella Giuntini and Dominique Barbolosi, with Cyril Voyant and David Taieb ( Scientific Reports , 2026). When a disease can be described by an intelligible model, that model comes first: it explains, it can be calibrated on real patients, and it lets one test protocols in silico . Artificial intelligence is not needed to do what the model already does well. 
 The question 
 Metastatic differentiated thyroid cancer is often treated with repeated sessions of radioactive iodine. Some tumours respond; others become refractory. Thyroglobulin (Tg), measured in the blood, follows the tumour burden. Which protocol, and for which patient profile? 
 The theory, in plain words 
 Three quantities evolve over the months: 
 the activity of the administered iodine decreases over time, and each session adds a new dose to what remains; 
 the tumour cells grow at a rate set by their doubling time T_d , and are killed in proportion to the activity present; 
 thyroglobulin is produced by the tumour cells and cleared by the body. 
 The equations are solved session by session, so a whole protocol can be simulated in seconds. A short doubling time means a fast-growing tumour: that is what separates a refractory profile from a responding one. 
 Where it sits on the complexity ladder 
 Complexity ladder: the thyroid model stops at the second rung, simulation from what is known 
 Second rung: simulation from a model we understand . The next step is a hybrid digital twin : keep the model, and let a learning method (a frugal extreme learning machine, for example) estimate only what the model does not capture. This is mathematics- and medicine-informed learning, not a black box replacing the model. No learning added where the model meets the need; learning, in hybrid form, where it helps. 
 The example in figures 
 Thyroglobulin over 80 months for 1, 2, 4 and 8 sessions, refractory and responding profiles 
 With the public demonstrator parameters, 3.7 GBq per session every 3 months: 
 Refractory profile ( T_d = 9.8 months): thyroglobulin reaches about 1,386 ng/mL at 79 months after one session, and stays near 12 ng/mL after eight. 
 Responding profile ( T_d = 66.6 months): about 14 ng/mL after one session, and 0.13 ng/mL after eight. 
 These are model outputs for two archetypes, not predictions for a patient. 
 What it brings, and its limits 
 Brings : an intelligible way to compare protocols before treating; a biomarker reading (the doubling time) that separates profiles; open code that anyone can run (MATLAB). 
 Limits : two archetypes and population-calibrated parameters; it is not a clinical decision tool and needs prospective validation. The learning part of the hybrid twin is work in progress, separate from the published results. 
 Go further 
 Article : M. Fusella Giuntini, C. Voyant, D. Taieb, D. Barbolosi, A computational framework for optimizing radioiodine therapy protocols in metastatic thyroid cancer, Scientific Reports 16, 27179 (2026), doi: 10.1038/s41598-026-56267-1 
 Full equations, results of the article and runnable code : https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/methods/thyroid-radioiodine.html 
 Code (RAIR-Sim) : github.com/MarieFG49/CTD_SIMU_RAI (MIT) · documented fork archived at doi: 10.5281/zenodo.21496198 
 Review : M. Fusella Giuntini, C. Voyant, D. Taieb, D. Barbolosi, Computational modeling and trends in RAI therapy for thyroid cancer, Biomedical Journal of Scientific & Technical Research 62(4) (2025), doi: 10.26717/BJSTR.2025.62.009789 
 For everyone (in French): "IA et cancer de la thyroïde : demain, la fin des traitements standardisés ?", The Conversation , May 2026 
 The approach behind this work : Understand before you compute
